mainTopic: A walker who breaks a jug left in the street, and whether a person may take the law into his own hands
overview: The amud begins by closing an earlier point: in money cases we do not follow the רוב (majority). Then the גמרא quotes the משנה that someone who trips over a jug left in the street and breaks it is פטור, and asks why, since he should have watched where he was going. רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן each describe a case where he could not avoid the jug, and רבי עולא adds that people simply do not watch the road. רב פפא and רבא argue over whether the word 'stumbled' in the משנה fits רב's explanation. Real court cases follow, where שמואל and רבא made the walker pay, and רב פפא explains that רבא's case was at an olive press, where jugs are put down with permission. A new topic then opens: רב חסדא asks רב נחמן about payment for a blow with a hoe. The facts reveal that the hitter was protecting his water, which leads to the dispute between רב יהודה and רב נחמן over whether a person may take the law into his own hands. רב כהנא challenges רב יהודה from בן בג בג, and רב יהודה's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: In money cases we do not follow the majority
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends the earlier discussion by saying the משנה teaches that in money matters we do not decide by the רוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is teaching us that in money matters we do not go after the majority.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is wrapping up the earlier discussion. It says the lesson of that part of the משנה is that we do not use the majority to decide money cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the רוב (majority) can settle a doubt. In ממון (money) cases it is not enough to take money from someone. The person who wants the money must bring proof.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us (the new point being made)

steps.whatToRemember: In money cases, the רוב alone does not take money away from someone. The claimant needs proof.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a major rule in דיני ממונות that comes up all over ש״ס.

phrases.english: It teaches us
that we do not go, in money matters,
after the majority.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion from the previous section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה teaches אין הולכין בממון אחר הרוב.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: the one who trips is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: if someone tripped over the jug and broke it, he is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If another person came, tripped on it and broke it, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה about a jug left in the public street. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is a jug that its owner left in רשות הרבים. A passerby trips on it and breaks it. The משנה says the passerby does not have to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.english: And another came and stumbled on it
phrases.notes: "It" is the jug that someone left in the public street, from the משנה.

phrases.english: and broke it — he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבָא אַחֵר וְנִתְקַל בָּהּ וּשְׁבָרָהּ פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by quoting the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who trips over a jug in רשות הרבים and breaks it is פטור.

steps.title: Why exempt? He should have looked
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the passerby is פטור, since he should have looked where he was walking.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is he exempt? He should have looked and then walked!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה's ruling. A careful person watches the road, so tripping looks like his own fault.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the jug should not have been there, the walker still has a duty to look ahead. If he could have seen it and avoided it, why shouldn't he pay for breaking it?

phrases.english: Why is he exempt?
He should have looked and then walked!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמַּאי פָּטוּר? אִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְעַיּוֹנֵי וּמֵיזַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling just quoted from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the one who trips is פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A walker is expected to watch the road. Tripping over something he could have seen should count as his own carelessness.

steps.title: רב: the whole street was filled with barrels
steps.stepSummary: The school of רב answers that the משנה is talking about someone who filled the entire street with barrels.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רב said in the name of רב: the case is where he filled the whole public street with barrels.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question. Looking would not have helped, because there was no way to get through without hitting barrels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the whole road was blocked, the walker had no choice. The public road belongs to everyone, so he may pass even if barrels break. The blame falls on the person who blocked the street.

phrases.english: The school of Rav said in the name of Rav:
It is where he fills the public domain
entirely with barrels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The walker could have looked and avoided the jug, so he should pay.
steps.terutzMaskana: The entire street was blocked, so even looking would not have let him pass without breaking barrels.

steps.title: שמואל: it happened in the dark
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers that the משנה is talking about a case that happened in the dark.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: the משנה was taught about a case in the dark.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a different answer to the same question. In the dark, the walker could not see the jug however carefully he looked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב kept the light and changed the road. שמואל keeps the single jug and says the walker could not see. Either way, the walker could not have avoided it, so he is not careless.

phrases.english: Shmuel said: They taught it about darkness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the question of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The walker could have looked and seen the jug.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was dark, so looking would not have helped.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the jug was at a corner
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that the jug was placed at a corner of the street.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: the case is where it was at a corner.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a third answer. The jug was around a corner, so the walker could not see it until it was too late.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like שמואל, רבי יוחנן says the walker could not see the jug, but for a different reason. As he turned the corner, the jug was right there.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said: At a corner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the question of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The walker could have looked and seen the jug.
steps.terutzMaskana: The jug was at a corner, out of sight, so he could not have avoided it.

steps.title: רב פפא: the משנה fits שמואל or רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the precise wording of the משנה fits only שמואל or רבי יוחנן, not רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: the משנה is precise only according to שמואל or רבי יוחנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא judges between the three answers. He claims the wording of the משנה matches שמואל or רבי יוחנן. His reason comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רב פפא only states his conclusion. He is checking which answer fits the exact words of the משנה. The proof follows right after.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Our mishnah is not precise

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אוֹ כִּשְׁמוּאֵל, אוֹ כְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן.
phrases.english: except either like Shmuel or like Rabbi Yochanan.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא לָא דַּיְקָא מַתְנִיתִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Weighs the three answers of steps 4 through 6 against the wording of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's wording fits שמואל or רבי יוחנן, not רב.

steps.title: Against רב: why say tripped?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains: if רב were right, the משנה would not need to say 'tripped', since even breaking on purpose would be פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if it is like רב, why specifically say 'tripped'? Even if he broke it on purpose he would also be exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives his proof against רב's reading. The word 'tripped' in the משנה would be unnecessary in רב's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב's case the barrel owner blocked the whole public road, so a walker may break through even on purpose. Then the משנה should not mention tripping at all. In שמואל's and רבי יוחנן's cases, only an accidental trip is פטור, so the word 'tripped' makes sense.
steps.confusionAlert: רב פפא is not saying that רב's ruling is wrong in law. He is only saying that the word 'tripped' in the משנה fits the other two answers better.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the גמרא tests an explanation by asking whether every word of the משנה has a purpose.

phrases.english: For if it is like Rav, why specifically 'stumbled'?
Even if he broke it, also!
phrases.notes: He means even breaking it on purpose, not just by tripping, would be exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind רב פפא's claim in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's explanation that the whole street was filled with barrels.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In רב's case even breaking on purpose would be פטור, so the משנה's word 'tripped' would be extra. That shows the משנה is talking about a case where only tripping is excused.

steps.title: רבא's defense: the word 'stumbled' is for the second half of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד, quoting רבא, answers רב פפא. Under רב's view, even breaking the barrel on purpose is פטור. The משנה says 'stumbled' only because the second half of the משנה needs that word.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: The same is true even if he broke it on purpose. The משנה says 'stumbled' because it wants to teach the second half: 'If he was hurt by it, the barrel owner must pay for his injury.' That is only true if he stumbled. If he broke it on purpose and got hurt, the owner does not pay, because he hurt himself. So the first half also says 'stumbled.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב פפא's challenge from Step 8. It shows that the word 'stumbled' in the משנה fits רב's explanation too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא said 'stumbled' proves רב is wrong, since under רב even breaking on purpose would be פטור. רבא agrees that breaking on purpose would be פטור. He explains that 'stumbled' is needed for the second half of the משנה: the barrel owner pays for the walker's injury only if the walker stumbled. If the walker broke the barrel on purpose and got hurt, he hurt himself.

keyTerms.meaning: Since / because (the משנה wanted to say something else nearby)
The last clause of the משנה
The first clause of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: The two halves of the משנה are about different damage. The first half is about the barrel breaking. The second half is about the walker getting hurt. Breaking on purpose makes no difference to the first half, but it makes a big difference to the second half.

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said in the name of Rava:
The same is true even if he broke it [on purpose];
and the fact that it teaches "stumbled" —
is because it wants to teach the last clause:
"And if he was injured by it —
the owner of the barrel is liable for his damage,"
which applies specifically when he stumbled, but if he broke it [on purpose] — no.
What is the reason? He is the one who damaged himself;
therefore it teaches "stumbled" in the first clause too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's wording challenge against רב (Step 8).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the משנה uses a certain word: 'stumbled' was written because the second half of the משנה needs it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'stumbled' seemed to mean that breaking on purpose would make him pay, which goes against רב.
steps.terutzMaskana: Under רב, breaking on purpose is also פטור. 'Stumbled' matters only for the second half, where the walker is hurt.

steps.title: רבי עולא's reason: people don't watch the road
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא reports in the name of רבי עולא that the walker is פטור because people do not usually look carefully at the road.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said to רב אשי: This is what they say in ארץ ישראל in the name of רבי עולא: The walker is פטור because people do not usually look carefully at the road as they walk.
steps.whatsHappening: A new explanation of the משנה arrives from ארץ ישראל. The walker is פטור even if the barrel could be seen, because people normally do not watch the road.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is different from the answers of רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן. It needs no special case like a full street, darkness or a corner. It says that walking without staring at the ground is normal, so the walker is not at fault. The burden falls on whoever put the barrel in the street.

keyTerms.meaning: In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל
To look carefully, to pay attention

steps.whyThisMatters: This explanation needs no special case to make the walker פטור. That sets up the question of how שמואל and רבא could make walkers pay in the real cases that come next.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב אָשֵׁי,
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said to Rav Ashi,
this is what they say in the West
phrases.notes: "The West" means ארץ ישראל, which is west of בבל.

phrases.english: in the name of Rabbi Ulla:

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין דַּרְכָּן שֶׁל בְּנֵי אָדָם
phrases.english: because it is not the way of people
to look carefully at the roads.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי אָמְרִי בְּמַעְרְבָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי עוּלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another reason for the משנה's פטור, different from the three answers already given.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The walker who stumbles is פטור because people normally do not watch the road.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A general reason, not a special case: people normally do not watch the road.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The walker could have looked and avoided the jug, so he should pay.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if the jug could be seen, people do not normally watch the road, so the walker is not at fault.

steps.title: Real cases: שמואל and רבא made the walker pay
steps.stepSummary: In real cases in נהרדעא and פומבדיתא, שמואל and רבא each made the person who broke the jug pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a case in נהרדעא, and שמואל made him pay. There was a case in פומבדיתא, and רבא made him pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells of two real court cases where someone broke a jug in the street and had to pay. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rulings seem to go against the משנה's פטור, so they must fit one of the explanations. For שמואל it is easy, because he limited the פטור to darkness. For רבא it is not clear yet.

keyTerms.meaning: An actual incident or court case
He ruled the person must pay

phrases.english: There was an incident in Neharde'a,
and Shmuel held him liable.
In Pumbedita, and Rava held him liable.
phrases.notes: The גמרא leaves it understood that this was the same kind of case: someone broke a jug left in the street.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining the משנה to real rulings that apply it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, שמואל and רבא made the person who broke the jug pay.

steps.title: Does רבא agree with שמואל?
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's ruling matches his own view. The גמרא asks whether רבא's ruling means he also holds like שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל's ruling makes sense, because it follows his own teaching. But רבא: shall we say he holds like שמואל?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what view רבא's ruling is based on. This question sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said the משנה's פטור is only in the dark (Step 5), so in daylight the walker pays. רבא made the walker pay too, which seems to put him on שמואל's side. The next step shows that רבא's ruling had a different basis.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense for (this one), but

phrases.english: It works out for Shmuel — he follows his own teaching.
phrases.notes: His teaching is from Step 5: the פטור is only when it happened in the dark.

phrases.english: But Rava —
shall we say he holds like Shmuel?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions רבא's ruling from Step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What view is רבא's ruling based on? Does he agree with שמואל that the פטור is only in the dark?

steps.title: רבא's case happened at an olive press, where walkers must look
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that רבא's ruling does not prove he holds like שמואל. His case happened at the corner of an olive press, where people put jugs down with permission, so the walker should have been watching.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: That case happened at the corner of an olive press. Since people put their jugs there with permission, the walker should have looked first and then walked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 12. רבא's ruling was based on a special place, not on agreeing with שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the jug has no business being in the street, so the walker is not expected to be on guard for it. Near an olive press, everyone knows people set jugs down while waiting for oil, and they are allowed to. So there the walker is expected to look. That makes רבא's ruling a special case, not proof that he holds like שמואל's general view.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא made the walker pay only because the case was near an olive press. There, putting jugs down is normal and allowed, so the walker must watch. This does not prove that רבא agrees with שמואל in general.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It was at the corner of the olive press,
phrases.notes: He means רבא's real case from step 11 happened at that spot.

phrases.english: since they act there with permission,
he should have looked carefully and then walked.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: קַרְנָא דְּעַצְרָא הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 12 by pointing to a special location.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. רבא's ruling was due to the olive-press location, where walkers are expected to look.

steps.title: רב חסדא asks about payment for hitting with a hoe
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא sends רב נחמן a question. The set payments for kneeing, kicking, and punching are known, but what does someone pay for hitting with the handle or top of a hoe?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא sent to רב נחמן: They have said that for kneeing someone the payment is three, for kicking five, and for punching thirteen. What is the payment for hitting with the handle of a hoe or the top of a hoe?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins here. רב חסדא lists known fixed payments for embarrassing hits and asks what the amount is for a hoe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חכמים set fixed amounts for certain shameful blows. A hoe is not on that list, so רב חסדא asks how much it would cost. The next step questions whether he should be collecting this kind of payment at all.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: Rav Chisda sent to Rav Nachman:
They have said:
for kneeing, three;
for kicking, five;
for punching, thirteen.
For the handle of a hoe and the top of a hoe, what is the payment?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the broken jug.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The fixed payment for hitting someone with the handle or top of a hoe.

steps.title: רב נחמן questions collecting fines and asks for the facts
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers sharply. Fines like these cannot be collected in בבל, so he asks רב חסדא to tell him what actually happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן sent back: חסדא, חסדא, are you collecting a fine in בבל? Tell me what actually happened in the case.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן does not give an amount. He questions whether the fine can be collected, and he asks for the real story. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These fixed amounts count as a קנס, which judges in בבל cannot collect. So the question as asked has no practical use. רב נחמן suspects the real facts may lead somewhere else, so he asks for the details.

keyTerms.meaning: a fine (a set penalty, not payment for an actual loss)

steps.confusionAlert: רב נחמן is not saying that hitting someone is allowed. He is only saying that a court in בבל cannot collect this kind of fixed fine.

phrases.english: He sent to him:
Chisda, Chisda,
are you collecting a fine in Babylonia?

phrases.aramaic: אֵימָא לִי גּוּפָא דְעוֹבָדָא הֵיכִי הֲוָה.
phrases.english: Tell me how the actual incident happened.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ: חִסְדָּא חִסְדָּא, קְנָסָא קָא מַגְבֵּית בְּבָבֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רב חסדא's question by questioning its premise.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No amount is given. Fines cannot be collected in בבל, and רב נחמן asks for the facts.

steps.title: The story of the shared cistern
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא describes the case. Two partners took turns drawing water from a cistern. One drew on the other's day and ignored his protest, so the other hit him with a hoe handle.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא sent back: There was a cistern owned by two people, and each day one of them drew water from it. One of them came and drew water on a day that was not his turn. The other said to him, "It is my day!" He ignored him. So the other took the handle of a hoe and hit him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives רב נחמן the facts he asked for. This sets up the question of whether the hitter has to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the key detail comes out. The hitter was protecting his own water from someone taking it on his day. This raises a new question that the גמרא will discuss next: may a person use force to protect what is his?

keyTerms.meaning: he paid no attention to him

steps.whyThisMatters: This story leads to the well-known question of whether a person may take the law into his own hands to protect his property.

phrases.english: He sent to him:
There was a certain cistern belonging to two people,

phrases.aramaic: דְּכׇל יוֹמָא הֲוָה דָּלֵי חַד מִנַּיְיהוּ.
phrases.english: where each day one of them would draw water.
One of them came and was drawing water
on a day that was not his.
The other said to him: It is my day!
He paid no attention to him.
So he took the handle of a hoe and struck him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ: דְּהָהוּא גַּרְגּוּתָא דְּבֵי תְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the facts that רב נחמן asked for.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Facts of the case: a partner hit his co-owner with a hoe handle to stop him from drawing water on the partner's day.

steps.title: רב נחמן says the partner was right to hit him
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that the injured partner could have hit him even a hundred times, because when there is a loss, everyone allows a person to enforce the law himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: He should have hit him even a hundred times with the hoe handle! Even according to the one who says a person may not take the law into his own hands, where there would be a loss, a person may take the law into his own hands.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן now responds to the real case רב חסדא described. He rules that the partner who used the hoe handle owes nothing, because he was allowed to defend his rights.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was how much the hitter must pay. רב נחמן flips it: the hitter acted properly. Even the strictest view, which says a person must go to court, agrees that he may act on his own when waiting would make him lose something, like his share of the water.

keyTerms.meaning: The handle of a hoe (the tool used in the hitting)
A person may take the law into his own hands (enforce his rights himself)
A loss, damage that would happen if he waited
According to the one who says

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key rule of the whole section. Where a loss is at stake, a person may protect his property himself, even with force.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מְאָה פַּנְדֵי בְּפַנְדָּא לִמְחֲיֵיהּ!
phrases.english: He said to him: He should have hit him a hundred blows with the hoe handle!
phrases.notes: This is רב נחמן speaking. He is saying the hitter was completely in the right.

phrases.english: Even according to the one who says:
A person may not take the law into his own hands;
in a place of loss,
a person may take the law into his own hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מְאָה פַּנְדֵי בְּפַנְדָּא לִמְחֲיֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רב נחמן's ruling on the actual case רב חסדא described in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the partner who hit with the hoe handle must pay.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Nothing. He was entitled to hit him, because one may enforce the law himself where there is a loss.

steps.title: The dispute between רב יהודה and רב נחמן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites the known dispute: רב יהודה says a person may not take the law into his own hands, and רב נחמן says he may.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was stated: רב יהודה says a person may not take the law into his own hands. רב נחמן says a person may take the law into his own hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source for the phrase "even according to the one who says" from the last step. It shows there really is a dispute on this topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the two opinions are stated with no limits at all. That raises an obvious question: how does this fit with the claim that everyone agrees when there is a loss? The next step will define exactly where they argue.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was stated (introduces a dispute between אמוראים)
The אמורא who holds one may not enforce the law himself
The אמורא who holds one may enforce the law himself

phrases.english: As it was stated: רב יהודה says:
A person may not take the law into his own hands.
רב נחמן says:
A person may take the law into his own hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the dispute that step 17 referred to with "the one who says."
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יהודה: a person may not take the law into his own hands. רב נחמן: he may.

steps.title: Defining where they really argue
steps.stepSummary: Where there is a loss, everyone allows self-enforcement. They argue only where there is no loss: רב יהודה says go to a judge, and רב נחמן says a person acting lawfully need not bother.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where there is a loss, everyone agrees a person may take the law into his own hands. They argue where there is no loss. רב יהודה says he may not, because since there is no loss, he should go before the judge. רב נחמן says he may, because since he is acting lawfully, he does not need to trouble himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the dispute from the last step. It explains that the two אמוראים disagree only in cases where waiting causes no loss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains how step 17 could say "even according to the one who says": with a loss, רב יהודה agrees. Without a loss, רב יהודה wants the person to go to court since he has time. רב נחמן says that if he is clearly in the right, the trip to court is unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees (literally, the whole world does not argue)

steps.whatToRemember: With a loss, everyone allows a person to enforce the law himself. Without a loss, רב יהודה says go to court and רב נחמן says he may act on his own if he is clearly right.

phrases.english: Where there is a loss,
everyone agrees
that a person may take the law into his own hands.
Where they argue is where there is no loss;
רב יהודה says:
A person may not take the law into his own hands,
because since there is no loss,
let him go before the judge.
רב נחמן says:
A person may take the law into his own hands,
because since he is acting according to the law,
he does not need to trouble himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא פְּסֵידָא כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the dispute from step 18 to cases with no loss, which fits step 17's claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With a loss, all allow self-enforcement. Without a loss, רב יהודה requires going to a judge and רב נחמן allows acting alone.

steps.title: רב כהנא challenges רב יהודה from בן בג בג
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא challenges רב יהודה with בן בג בג's teaching: do not sneak into a friend's yard to take your item, but take it openly, even by force, saying "I am taking what is mine."
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא raised an objection. בן בג בג says: Do not enter your friend's courtyard to take what is yours without permission, so that you do not look like a thief to him. Rather, break his teeth and say to him: I am taking what is mine.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא attacks רב יהודה's view with an earlier teaching. That teaching seems to allow a person to take his own item by force, even with no loss involved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בן בג בג's case has no sign of a loss, yet he tells the owner to take back his item himself, forcefully and openly. That fits רב נחמן and seems to contradict רב יהודה, who said that without a loss one must go to a judge.

keyTerms.meaning: He raises an objection (challenges from an earlier source)
A תנא whose teaching is quoted here

steps.confusionAlert: "Break his teeth" is strong language for taking your item openly by force. It is not literal advice to injure someone.

phrases.english: רב כהנא raised an objection:
phrases.notes: The challenge is aimed at רב יהודה, who said that without a loss you must go to a judge.

phrases.english: בן בג בג says:
Do not enter your friend's courtyard
to take what is yours without permission,
lest you appear to him like a thief.
Rather, break his teeth,
and say to him: I am taking what is mine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יהודה's position as it was defined in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's view that, when there is no loss, a person may not take the law into his own hands.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: בן בג בג tells a person to take his own item from another's yard by force, with no loss mentioned. That means self-enforcement is allowed even without a loss.

steps.title: רב יהודה begins his reply to רב כהנא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces רב יהודה's response to רב כהנא's challenge from בן בג בג. Only the opening formula appears here, and the answer itself continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said to him (to רב כהנא):
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up רב יהודה's answer to the challenge from בן בג בג. These words only open the reply, and the real answer continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא's question was strong: בן בג בג seems to allow a person to take his own item by force, which looks like the opposite of רב יהודה's view. The words אֲמַר לֵיהּ tell us that רב יהודה is not dropping his position. He is about to defend it.

keyTerms.meaning: "He said to him". This formula opens a direct reply to the person who just spoke.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the answer is missing. These words only open רב יהודה's reply, and the content of his answer continues on the next amud.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: "He" is רב יהודה, answering רב כהנא's challenge from בן בג בג.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens רב יהודה's defense against the קשיא raised by רב כהנא in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defense of רב יהודה's position. The specific resolution continues on the next amud.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: בן בג בג's teaching seems to allow self-enforcement even where there is no loss, which would contradict רב יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Not yet stated here. רב יהודה's answer continues on the next amud.
